ABSTRACT

Detached breakwaters are widely used as coastal protection structures to mitigate the shoreline erosion by reducing the wave energy reaching the coast. The previous studies have primarily focused on the shoreline evolution or on the empirical prediction, whereas the coupled hydrodynamic–morphodynamic processes linking wave characteristics, gap geometry, and the shoreline response have not been explained comprehensively. This study aims to investigate the shoreline morphodynamic response induced by the wave–gap interaction and to develop the process-based empirical equations for predicting the shoreline response by using a three-dimensional movable-bed physical model. The results demonstrate that the shoreline morphodynamic response is governed by a hierarchical hydrodynamic–morphodynamic mechanism. The wave propagation and wave–gap interaction regulate the wave energy transmission and redistribution behind the detached breakwaters, leading to the formation of induced circulation that subsequently controls the sediment transport and shoreline adjustment. Based on this mechanism, two empirical equations were developed for the different engineering applications: a preliminary design equation by using 𝐻𝑔𝑇2 and 𝛥𝑔𝑔𝑇2, and a performance evaluation equation incorporating the Froude number 𝐹𝑟as the hydrodynamic mediator. These findings establish a process-based mechanistic framework for interpreting the shoreline morphodynamic response and provide two empirical equations that support the planning and performance evaluation of detached breakwaters.
